sections.section_title: 1.1 The concept of democracy and democratization

slides.title: Understanding Democracy
content: No absolute definition of democracy exists.
The term is elastic and expands or contracts based on time, place, and circumstances.
It covers a wide range of political systems, from old established ones to new, inexperienced ones.
Etymology: Derived from Greek words 'Demo' (people) and 'Kratos' (rule).
Basic meaning: Rule by the people or government by the people.

slides.title: Key Concepts in Democracy
content: A democratic system is one in which citizens freely make political decisions by majority rule.
A dictionary definition: State of government where people hold ruling power directly or through elected representatives.
Embraces principles of equality, individual freedom, and opportunity for common people.
State power involves compromise and bargaining in the decision-making process.
Activity: Discuss how democracy is practiced in your local community.

sections.section_title: 1.2 Definitions and actors of democratization process

slides.title: Understanding Democratization
content: Democratization is a complex, long-term, dynamic, and open-ended process.
It is a political process that moves a country's political system towards democracy.
It can be a transition from authoritarian to semi-democracy, or from semi-authoritarian to full democracy.
Democracy is not an overnight program; it requires time and different actors.

slides.title: Actors in the Democratization Process: Political Parties
content: Political parties are essential to the functioning and durability of democracy.
They are the instruments through which power is attained via free, fair, and transparent elections.
They are settings for working out practical ideas and proposals for alternative government programs.
Key function: They serve as a machinery for recruitment and appointment of leaders.

slides.title: Actors in the Democratization Process: Media
content: Freedom of the media is essential in a democracy.
Media includes newspapers, television, radio, books, magazines, cinema, and social media.
Plays a role in the political training of citizens and building democratic culture.
To perform these functions, media must be free, independent, and well-resourced.
Importance lies in the quality of information provided, not just the quantity.

slides.title: Importance of Democratic Institutions
content: Democratic institutions are important to develop and protect democracy.
These institutions must serve the entire population with equality under the law.
Strong institutions are respected and become difficult to manipulate.
They enable honest people to survive.

slides.title: Democratic Institutions: INEC
content: Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC)
A corporate body charged with organizing, conducting, and supervising elections.
Functions include: conducting elections and referendums, registering voters, delimiting constituencies, registering political parties, and educating the electorate.

slides.title: Democratic Institutions: Political Parties
content: Organized groups of individuals who share political ideologies, beliefs, and interests.
Seek to win elections and control state power.
Functions: Forum for national unity, educating the public, linking people and government, ensuring political stability, and holding the party in power accountable.

slides.title: Democratic Institutions: Pressure Groups
content: Organized body of people seeking to influence government policy.
Also known as interest groups.
Functions: Offering advice, promoting economic stability, educating the public, acting as a watchdog, and supporting candidates.
Example: Trade unions, business associations.

sections.section_title: 1.4 The role of democracy for social transformation

slides.title: Social Transformation
content: Social transformation is the restructuring of all aspects of life.
It includes culture, social relations, politics, economy, and ways of thinking.
Societies have transformed from small associations to communities, to nations tied by history, politics, and laws.
Democracy can play a significant role in facilitating this process.

slides.title: Dimensions of Social Transformation
content: Social Change: Range of outcomes from increased awareness to policy change correcting injustice.
Civic Engagement: Participation in civic, community, and political life to improve one's community.
Civic Dialogue: Exploring matters of civic importance with differing viewpoints to build understanding.
Social Capital: Collective value of social networks, trust, reciprocity, and cooperation.
Community Development: Empowering individuals and groups with skills and resources to effect change.

slides.title: Core Democratic Values
content: Liberty, Justice, and Equality are the core values central to democracy.
Liberty: Personal, political, and economic freedoms.
Justice: Distributive, corrective, and procedural fairness.
Equality: Political, social, and economic equality.

slides.title: Liberty
content: Personal Freedom: Free from arbitrary arrest, detention, and unreasonable searches.
Political Freedom: Right to participate freely in the political process.
Economic Freedom: Right to acquire, use, transfer, and dispose of private property; right to seek employment.

slides.title: Justice and Equality
content: Justice:
- Distributive Justice: Fair distribution of benefits and burdens.
- Corrective Justice: Proportional response to correct wrongs.
- Procedural Justice: Impartial and open decision-making.
Equality:
- Political Equality: Equal political rights (one person, one vote).
- Social Equality: No social hierarchy or discrimination.
- Economic Equality: Equal and fair access to national resources.

slides.title: Aspects of Democracy
content: Social Aspect: Removal of discrimination based on class, caste, creed, color, sex, ethnicity.
Economic Aspect: Equitable distribution of wealth, abolition of disparities, rights to work, leisure, and fair wages.
Political Aspect: Provision of political rights like voting, contesting elections, holding public office, freedom of movement, thought, association, and speech.

units.unit_title: Citizens in the Digital Technology Age

sections.section_title: 2.1 Implications of digital technology on citizens

slides.title: Overview: Implications of Digital Technology
content: Digital technologies have advanced rapidly and impact citizens' emotions, social life, and ethical values.
Moderate use leads to positive effects.
Excessive, addictive use leads to negative effects.

slides.title: Positive Implications on Emotions
content: Self-control: Enables people to manage and express emotions, especially in workplace.
Fostering Socialization: Improves interpersonal relationships and strengthens social bonds.
Maintaining Emotional Balance: Helps cope with stress and coordinate everyday activities.
Supporting Happiness and Wellbeing: Boosts health through social connection and creativity.
Regulating Emotions: Provides access to health resources to build skills like mindfulness.
Providing a Sense of Security: Mobile phones give a sense of security in public spaces.

slides.title: Negative Implications on Emotions
content: Isolation: Higher social media use linked to feeling socially isolated.
Secondhand Living: Living life through digital media rather than firsthand experience.
Depression and Anxiety: More online interactions can lead to higher levels of depression.
Anonymity and Fake Personality: People hide identities and behave anti-socially.
Addiction: Social media, gaming, and messaging can become addictive.

slides.title: Positive Implications on Social Life
content: Increased Social Connectivity: Social media and mobile phones enable new connections.
Speedy Communication: Fast broadband enables real-time video/audio and large data transfers.
Advancing Education: Enables sharing of academic information and virtual learning.
Facilitating Transportation: Online booking, digital chips in passports.
Advancing Banking and Finance: Online banking and international money transfers.
Improving Health Care: Access to diagnostic tools, medical records, and remote consultations.
Promoting Economic Growth: New innovations and increased agricultural productivity.

slides.title: Negative Implications on Social Life
content: Social Alienation: People socialize via digital devices instead of real-life contact.
Eroding Privacy: Harder to keep personal data safe; photos and footage can be posted online.
Replacing Human Jobs: Remote work allows undercutting, computers replace humans.
Data Insecurity: Large amounts of data can be collected and stolen.
Aggravate Crime and Terrorism: Terrorists and criminals use the internet for operations.
Effects on Physical Health: Eyestrain, poor posture, and musculoskeletal problems.

slides.title: Positive Implications on Ethical Values
content: Developing Critical Thinking: Access to diverse sources allows analysis and challenging of information.
Developing Universal Moral Values: Interaction with others helps compare and contrast moral norms.
Self-learning of Good Habits: Learning from the life experiences of philosophers and others.

slides.title: Negative Implications on Ethical Values
content: Ethical Dilemma: Access to different philosophical thoughts can lead to confusion.
Increasing Uncertainty: Many ethical issues debated online lead to confusion.
Creating Unhappiness: Social media can contain vulgar and offending messages.
Untruthfulness: Spread of fake information and news.
Eroding Norms of Freedom: Fear of insult prevents free expression.
Induction of Negative Emotions: Exposure to sad or violent content increases fear and anger.

sections.section_title: 2.2 The ethics of using digital technology

slides.title: Ethics of Digital Technology
content: There is an increasing trend of misuse and abuse of emerging digital technologies.
Ethical codes of conduct are important to guide behavior.
Common ethical codes include: Etiquette, Responsibility, Safety, Security, Confidentiality, and Accuracy.

slides.title: Ethical Codes of Digital Technology
content: Etiquette: Understanding how digital behavior affects others; being a role model.
Responsibility: Thinking twice about what is appropriate, ethical, and legal to download.
Safety: Being aware of physical dangers like eyestrain and poor posture.
Security: Protecting electronic data and equipment from viruses and unauthorized access.
Confidentiality: Protecting personal privacy and passwords.
Accuracy/Trustworthiness: Ensuring information is correct; citing sources.

sections.section_title: 2.3 Opportunities of digital technology for young citizens

slides.title: Opportunities for Young Citizens
content: Information Access: Easy access to local and global events.
Social Connectivity: Empowers young people to participate in the digital world.
Learning Opportunities: Access to world knowledge, online lessons, and courses.
Versatile Working Opportunities: Remote working and easy online job searches.
Innovation and Creative Opportunities: Exposure to new ideas fosters creativity and innovation.

sections.section_title: 2.4 Impacts of unethical use of digital technology on young citizens

slides.title: Impacts of Unethical Digital Use
content: Academic Dishonesty: Cheating and plagiarism make students dependent and unanalytical.
Digital Media Piracy: Illegal circulation of music, movies, and books violates property rights.
Identity Theft: People hide behind fake personas to commit scams and fraud.
Unfriendly and Revenge Sex: Exposure to inappropriate content leads to relationship problems and addiction.

slides.title: What is Good Governance?
content: Refers to the processes, institutions, and practices through which common concerns are decided and regulated.
Measures how public institutions conduct affairs and manage resources efficiently.
Requires an efficient public service, a reliable judicial system, and an accountable administration.
Occurs when societal norms empower people to take control of their development without impinging on others' rights.

slides.title: Elements of Good Governance
content: Accountability: Officials must be answerable for their decisions.
Participation: Citizens must be involved in decision-making.
Rule of Law: Laws must be fair and enforced impartially.
Transparency: Information must be freely available and accessible.
Equity and Inclusiveness: All members of society must feel they have a stake.
Responsiveness: Serving stakeholders within a reasonable time.
Consensus Oriented: Mediating differing interests for broad consensus.
Effectiveness and Efficiency: Meeting society's needs while using resources optimally.

slides.title: Key Principles of Good Governance
content: Accountability, Participation, and Rule of Law are fundamental.
Transparency, Equity, and Inclusiveness ensure fair processes.
Responsiveness, Consensus, and Efficiency ensure effective service delivery.
All elements are interrelated; a problem in one compromises the effectiveness of others.

slides.title: Roles of Good Governance
content: Promoting Economic Development: Through rule of law, efficiency, and better resource allocation.
Improve Social Development: Enhancing living standards, health, education, and public participation.
Strengthen Social Cohesion: Ensuring all people have a stake and mediating diverse opinions.
Promoting Peace: Providing pathways for representation and addressing grievances.
Ensuring Social Justice: Impartial enforcement of the rule of law.
Enhancing Government Performance: Through accountability and responsiveness.
Ensuring Respect for Human Rights: Creating a prerequisite environment for their protection.

slides.title: Challenges for Good Governance
content: Poverty: Prevents people from focusing on participation and rights; leads to exclusion.
Corruption: Distorts economic systems, undermines social confidence, and creates injustice.
Corruption damages the development process and reinforces power relationships.
Weak rule of law makes it easier for leaders to mobilize violence and facilitates electoral fraud.

sections.section_title: 3.5 Impacts of lack of good governance

slides.title: Impacts of Lack of Good Governance
content: Political Instability: Governments that don't represent the public face unrest.
Inability of Rule of Law: Leads to manipulation of laws.
Inability to Secure Justice: Due to unfair resource distribution.
Lack of Transparency: Leads to public distrust.
Lack of Empowerment: Citizens' voices are not heard.
Inefficient Service Delivery: Poor standards and corruption in health and education.
Administrative Irregularities: Poor management.

slides.title: Understanding Corruption
content: Corruption: Misuse of public office for private gain.
Forms of corruption: Bribery, embezzlement, fraud, nepotism, extortion.
It erodes trust, weakens democracy, and hampers economic development.

slides.title: Ways of Fighting Corruption
content: Creating Public Awareness: Educating people about the damaging consequences.
Citizen Participation: Facilitating accountability and transparency.
Strengthening the Civil Service: Depoliticization and professionalization.
Increasing Accountability and Transparency: Making information accessible.
Simplifying Administrative Procedures: Reducing complexity.
Media: Raising awareness, investigating, and exposing corruption.
Strengthening the Judicial System: Ensuring laws are enforced.

units.unit_title: Peace and Indigenous Conflict Resolution Mechanisms

slides.title: What is Peace?
content: A state of mutual harmony between people or groups.
Internal (Inner) Peace: A state of calm and peacefulness of mind.
External Peace: The absence of war, disorder, and hostility; presence of social harmony and justice.
Positive Peace: True, lasting peace built on justice, eliminating root causes of violence.
Negative Peace: Absence of direct violence, but often without justice and with unresolved conflict.

slides.title: Impacts of Absence of Peace
content: Security Impacts: Direct and structural violence, cycles of violent conflict.
Social and Political Disharmony: Destroys national unity and creates suspicion and hatred.
Failure to Accommodate Cultural Diversity: Groups compete for power and resources.
Undermine Socio-Economic Development: Diverting resources to military spending.
Grave Human Rights Violations: Women and children are especially vulnerable to violence, abuse, and displacement.

slides.title: Peace Building
content: A long-term process of ensuring sustainable peace.
Encouraging conflicting parties to talk and understand each other.
Addressing root causes of conflict and creating viable institutions.
Transforming social institutions that reproduce violence.
Promoting integration of alienated groups.
Creating an environment for peaceful conflict resolution and preventing future violence.

slides.title: Indigenous Conflict Resolution Mechanisms
content: Grassroots, community-based practices for resolving conflicts according to customary norms.
Features: Context-specific, voluntary, consensus-based, flexible norms.
Goal: Restoration and maintenance of peaceful coexistence.
Involves negotiation, compromise, forgiveness, and compensation.
Examples: Makabanna (Afar), Shimagille (Amhara), Jarsumma (Oromo).

sections.section_title: 4.5 The roles of indigenous social institutions in ensuring sustainable peace

slides.title: Roles of Indigenous Institutions
content: Building Community Cohesion: Fostering solidarity and self-governance.
Restoring Order and Relationships: Focusing on reconciliation, not punishment.
Addressing Psycho-Social and Spiritual Dimensions: Providing rituals and healing.
Ensuring Inclusion and Participation: Consensus-based solutions.
Providing Accessibility: Offering immediate, context-sensitive solutions.

slides.title: What is Federalism?
content: A system of government where power is divided between a federal and regional governments.
Devolution: The principle of transferring power to regions.
Neither level is constitutionally subordinate to the other.
Each level has sovereign powers derived from the constitution.
A high federal court adjudicates disputes concerning federalism.

slides.title: Types of Federalism
content: Dual Federalism (Layer Cake): Clear division of powers between state and national governments.
- Advantages: Protects local jurisdictions, laws reflect local needs.
- Disadvantages: Tension, reduced cooperation, decreased unity.
Cooperative Federalism (Marble Cake): Shared power and collaboration on overlapping functions.
- Advantages: Efficient service delivery, practical cooperation.
- Disadvantages: Decrease in state powers, potential federal overreach.

slides.title: Key Features of Federalism
content: Division of Power: Political power is constitutionally divided between the federal and state governments.
Decentralized System: States derive authority from the constitution, not from the center.
Written and Supreme Constitution: Serves as the supreme law and clearly defines the division of powers.

slides.title: Advantages of Federalism
content: Division of powers.
Separate governments.
Written and rigid constitution.
Special judiciary.
Better understanding of local issues.
Increasing citizen participation.
Protection against tyranny.
More efficiency.

slides.title: Disadvantages of Federalism
content: Conflict of authority.
Regionalism over patriotism.
Lack of accountability.
Inequalities between states.
States blocking nationalist policies.

sections.section_title: 5.5 The roles of federalism in accommodating diversity in Ethiopia

slides.title: Federalism in Ethiopia
content: Rationale: To reconcile ethnic diversity with political unity.
Shift from a historically centralized unitary state.
FDRE constitution lists federal, state, and concurrent powers, leaving residual power to states.
Bi-cameral legislature: House of Peoples' Representatives (supreme political organ) and House of Federation (interprets constitution).
Challenges: Balancing unity and diversity, making constituent units viable, managing individual vs. collective rights.

slides.title: What are Human Rights?
content: Fundamental entitlements belonging to every human being without discrimination.
Derived from human dignity and worth.
Provide minimum standards for a worth-living life.

slides.title: Basic Features of Human Rights
content: Universalism: Apply equally to all people everywhere.
Eternality: End only at natural death.
Inalienability: Cannot be given up or taken away.
Indivisible and Interdependent: One right depends on others.
Inviolability: Should not be violated.
Irrevocable: Cannot be taken away by any power.

slides.title: Classification of Human Rights
content: First Generation: Civil and political rights (e.g., freedom from discrimination, right to a fair trial).
Second Generation: Economic, social, and cultural rights (e.g., right to work, right to education).
Third Generation: Solidarity rights (e.g., right to self-determination, right to development).
FDRE constitution has a third of its provisions devoted to human rights and democratic rights.

sections.section_title: 6.2 Citizens and state obligations in realizing human rights

slides.title: Obligations for Human Rights
content: Citizens' Obligations: Respecting religious and gender equality, respecting the rights of others, and respecting national symbols.
State Obligations:
- Obligation to Respect: Refrain from interfering with rights.
- Obligation to Protect: Protect individuals from abuses by third parties.
- Obligation to Fulfill: Take positive action to ensure rights are realized.

slides.title: Instruments for Human Rights Protection
content: Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) - 1948.
International Conventions: ICCPR, ICESCR, CEDAW, CRC.
Regional Mechanisms in Africa, Americas, and Europe.
FDRE Constitution: Foundation of human rights in Ethiopia.
Ethiopian institutions: National Human Rights Commission, Ombudsman.

slides.title: What is Patriotism?
content: A sentiment and psychological attachment to one's nation.
Originates from the Latin word 'patria' meaning fatherland.
Love, devotion, and a sense of attachment to a homeland.
A feeling of pride in a country's history, culture, and tradition.
Action-oriented: expressed through devotion to the nation's fundamental values and principles.
In a democracy, it means devoting time, ability, and even life for the nation's security and welfare.

slides.title: Types of Patriotism
content: Constitutional Patriotism: Commitment to democracy, human rights, coexistence, and tolerance.
Traditional Patriotism: Readiness to give one's life for the motherland.
Icon Patriotism: Showing love through heroic or impactful actions.
Symbolic Patriotism: Respect for national symbols like the flag and anthem.
Capital Patriotism: Contributing to the development of the national economy.
Environmental Patriotism: Love for the country's environment and actions to protect it.

slides.title: Bases of Patriotism
content: Equality: Based on respect for constitutional democracy and human rights.
Tolerance: Accepting diversity as a civic obligation.
Loyalty: Loyalty to the constitution, the people, and the government.
Concern for Well-being: Readiness to defend the country.
Sacrificing Personal Desires: Sacrificing personal interests for the common good.
Protecting the Constitution: Supporting its implementation.
Carrying out Duties: Fulfilling personal and civic responsibilities.
Defending the Country: From external aggressors.

slides.title: Importance and Traits of Patriotism
content: Importance:
- Brings people together, fostering unity.
- Builds a stronger nation.
- Develops a spirit of pride.
Traits of Patriotic Citizens:
- Aware of rights and duties.
- Fight for a better nation.
- Eager to make the country better.
- Do not take undue advantage of privileges.

slides.title: Duties of Patriots
content: Knowing the True History: To develop a clear understanding and foster tolerance.
Promoting the Common Good: Subordinating personal interests and defending state secrets.
Poverty Reduction: Working to reduce poverty, as it weakens democracy.
Voluntarism: Taking personal initiatives to serve the community.
Factors Affecting the Common Good: Selfish interests and corruption.

slides.title: What is Globalization?
content: The multiplicity of linkages and interconnections between states and societies.
Events in one part of the world can have significant consequences elsewhere.
Often refers to economic globalization: integration of national economies into the international economy.
Dimensions:
- Political: Intensification of political interrelations.
- Economic: Increasing interdependence of economies.
- Social: Sharing of ideas and information.
- Cultural: Circulation and sharing of ideas, meanings, and values.

slides.title: Advantages of Globalization
content: Economic: Increased trade, economic growth, technological development.
Political: Information sharing, promotion of democratic principles.
Social: Transformations in society, access to information.
Cultural: Cultural exchange, multiculturalism.
Financial: Easier capital exchange, global financial markets.

slides.title: Disadvantages of Globalization
content: Cultural: Homogenization of cultures, loss of local traditions.
Political: Pressure on leaders, fragmentation of national consciousness.
Economic: Income inequality, marginalization of developing economies.
Social: Personal insecurity (crime), job insecurity, health insecurity, environmental insecurity.

sections.section_title: 8.3 Fighting the negative impact of globalization

slides.title: Fighting Negative Impacts
content: Promoting Indigenous Knowledge: Incorporating it into education systems.
Valuing Community Development: Community-driven projects are more effective.
Promoting Indigenous Social Welfare Programs: Reducing vulnerability to external intervention.
Regional Cooperation: Groups of nations solving common problems.
Providing an Innovation Fund: Encouraging innovations for developing countries.

slides.title: What are Global Issues?
content: Issues that affect large parts of the globe and are urgent.
Examples: Climate change, poverty, inequality, population explosion, unemployment, disease, terrorism.
Criteria: Extent, urgency, and centrality.

slides.title: Major Global Issues
content: Climate Change: Caused by industrialization, population growth, urbanization, leading to global warming.
Poverty and Inequality: Widespread, creating a cycle of deprivation and instability.
Population Explosion: Rapid population increase putting pressure on resources.
Unemployment: Leads to poverty, social exclusion, and instability.
Disease: Spread facilitated by travel and migration (e.g., HIV/AIDS, COVID-19).
Terrorism: Use of violence against civilians for political purposes, a global security threat.
